FireEye CEO says U.S. malware is more restrained than adversaries' Kevin Mandia speaks May 31, 2018 at the Cyber Threat Intelligence Forum presented by FireEye and produced by CyberScoop and FedScoop. (CyberScoop) Share Written by Zaid Shoorbajee Jun 1, 2018 | CyberScoop Written by Zaid Shoorbajee Jun 1, 2018 | CYBERSCOOP Malware used by the United States in offensive cyber-operations plays \xe2\x80\x9cnice\xe2\x80\x9d when compared to other nation-state malware, according to FireEye CEO Kevin Mandia. Speaking at the Cyber Threat Intelligence Forum produced by Scoop News Group on Thursday, Mandia said when FireEye analyzes malware from state-backed hackers, the company usually finds\xc2 elements of public policy baked into operations. Certain tells in the malware\xe2\x80\x99s behavior or the code itself can be indicative of which state is behind it. \xe2\x80\x9cWe find malware that sometimes has a time to live and then it doesn\xe2\x80\x99t run anymore. I wonder who would do that,\xe2\x80\x9d Mandia said on stage. \xe2\x80\x9cProbably [the U.S.] because we\xe2\x80\x99re the nicest hackers in cyberspace, besides maybe China.\xe2\x80\x9d The U.S. and China are more disciplined in their operations than adversaries like North Korea and Russia, who are instead unrestrained, he said. \xe2\x80\x9cWe see guardrails on malware from nations like the United States, but do we see guardrails on malware from Russia? No.\xe2\x80\x9d Other experts, including former U.S. officials, contend that the U.S. can be similarly unrestrained and careless in cyberspace. They point to one specific case that\xe2\x80\x99s widely attributed to the U.S. known as \xe2\x80\x9cStuxnet,\xe2\x80\x9d which originally targeted but quickly spread beyond an Iranian nuclear enrichment facility. Mandia went on to describe an unspecified North Korean cyber-operation that when it detected someone was investigating, the malware rewrote the victim\xe2\x80\x99s hard drive. Such properties are indicative of North Korea\xe2\x80\x99s attitude toward systems they compromise, Mandia said. \xe2\x80\x9cThat\xe2\x80\x99s annoying to deal with, but that\xe2\x80\x99s a policy decision. They don\xe2\x80\x99t care what they destroy when they compromise something,\xe2\x80\x9d he said. \xe2\x80\x9cAnd I have a funny suspicion with our lawyers looking over their shoulders with all of our offensive capability, we absolutely do care and we\xe2\x80\x99re not going to have collateral damage in cyberspace.\xe2\x80\x9d Mandia told CyberScoop in an interview after his keynote that the U.S.\xe2\x80\x99s behavior could change soon. CyberScoop recently reported that officials inside the National Security Council are pressing for more offensive measures on the heels of U.S. Cyber Command\xe2\x80\x99s recent elevation to a fully independent combatant command. \xe2\x80\x9cMy gut, just pure gut, not fact based \xe2\x80\x94 [U.S. Cyber Command] will probably break the niceties,\xe2\x80\x9d Mandia told CyberScoop. \xe2\x80\x9cIn cyberspace, everyone else is breaking [laws]. Nobody wants to over escalate, however the next war will be fought with a cyber component. We\xe2\x80\x99ll have to be ready for that.\xe2\x80\x9d The public remarks cracked a window into how U.S. cybersecurity companies deal with malware that appears to originate from the U.S. or allied governments. Mandia, for example, told CyberScoop that before publishing a public threat intelligence report, FireEye will typically tip off intelligence officials from the Five Eyes alliance\xc2 about the release. If FireEye detects malware on a customer\xe2\x80\x99s system that researchers think is from the U.S. or an allied country, it will remove it. But Mandia said such malware ought to be stealthier. \xe2\x80\x9cIf friendlies get caught by our detection, then in my opinion is they just need to get better,\xe2\x80\x9d Mandia said. \xe2\x80\x9cWe\xe2\x80\x99re going to protect our clients first and foremost.\xe2\x80\x9d In March, Russian cybersecurity company Kaspersky Lab released information on a operation referred to as \xe2\x80\x9cSlingshot,\xe2\x80\x9d which covered malware that was spying on victims located in the Middle East. As CyberScoop previously reported, Slingshot was a U.S. counterterrorism operation aimed at capturing terrorism targets. Kaspersky\xe2\x80\x99s report subsequently burned the operation. In a press briefing, FireEye executives said that the company treats all cyberthreats the same, but uses discretion when it comes to public disclosure. \xe2\x80\x9cWe respond to breaches all over the world. There are certain times when we think it\xe2\x80\x99s potentially a friendly that was behind it,\xe2\x80\x9d said Charles Carmakal, a vice president with Mandiant, FireEye\xe2\x80\x99s incident response subsidiary. \xe2\x80\x9cFrom our investigative perspective we treat it as if it was a threat actor. We help our clients eradicate the threat actor from their environment.\xe2\x80\x9d But even with removing a threat from a customer\xe2\x80\x99s system, officials said the company would stop short of going public. Ron Bushar, a vice president at FireEye, compared the action to publicly disclosing a zero-day vulnerability without giving the affected organization a chance to fix the issue. \xe2\x80\x9cI think there\xe2\x80\x99s a difference between public disclosure and investigative support, and I think there\xe2\x80\x99s important standards or best practices that we tend to follow,\xe2\x80\x9d Bushar said. \xe2\x80\x9cAnd certainly before you go public with anything \xe2\x80\xa6 there has to be a consideration of what the impacts are both from a government perspective and what those impact could be to your client and to the organization conducting those operations.\xe2\x80\x9d Another FireEye executive, John Hultquist, director of threat analysis, said that publicly outing a U.S. cyber-espionage operation, especially a counterterrorism effort, would cross a line that goes beyond quietly dealing with the issue for a client. \xe2\x80\x9cI see counter terrorism stuff all the time,\xe2\x80\x9d said Hultquist. \xe2\x80\x9cThere\xe2\x80\x99s a difference, you know, between stopping it and publishing it for everyone to see.\xe2\x80\x9d Greg Otto and Chris Bing contributed to this report.\xc2 -In this Story- Cyber Threat Intelligence Forum, FireEye, Five Eyes, Kevin Mandia, malware, Mandiant, zero-days Related news Government U.S. files civil suit... by Shannon Vavra \xe2\x80\xa2 5 hours ago Government U.S. cyber-offensive... by Shannon Vavra \xe2\x80\xa2 8 hours ago Government Hacked government... by Sean Lyngaas \xe2\x80\xa2 1 day ago Ad Specs Sponsor RSS Privacy Policy \xc2\xa9 2019 Scoop News Group | All Rights Reserved Search for: The best cybersecurity news, delivered straight to your inbox.
